entries.4285055821916637b83ffe606bda527abf61dc90: <div sID="gen19793" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="7" osisID="Hos.7" sID="Hos.7"/> <div eID="gen19793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19794" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19795" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. A general charge drawn up against Israel for those high crimes and misdemeanors by which they had obstructed the course of God's favours to them, <reference osisRef="Hos.7.1-Hos.7.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. A particular accusation, 1. Of the court—the king, princes, and judges, <reference osisRef="Hos.7.3-Hos.7.7">ver. 3-7</reference>. 2. Of the country. Ephraim is here charged with conforming to the nations (<reference osisRef="Hos.7.8">ver. 8</reference>), senselessness and stupidity under the judgments of God (<reference osisRef="Hos.7.9-Hos.7.11">ver. 9-11</reference>), ingratitude to God for his mercies (<reference osisRef="Hos.7.13">ver. 13</reference>), incorrigibleness under his judgments (<reference osisRef="Hos.7.14">ver. 14</reference>), contempt of God (<reference osisRef="Hos.7.15">ver. 15</reference>), and hypocrisy in their pretences to return to him, <reference osisRef="Hos.7.16">ver. 16</reference>. They are also threatened with a severe chastisement, which shall humble them (<reference osisRef="Hos.7.12">ver. 12</reference>), and, if that prevail not, then with an utter destruction (<reference osisRef="Hos.7.13">ver. 13</reference>), particularly their princes, <reference osisRef="Hos.7.16">ver. 16</reference>.
entries.d02c911c33e5c96df93d886737ed9c108f57e7bb: <div eID="gen19795" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19794" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Charge Drawn up against Israel; The Crimes of the Princes. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 750.)</title> <div sID="gen19796" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> When I would have healed Israel, then the iniquity of Ephraim was discovered, and the wickedness of Samaria: for they commit falsehood; and the thief cometh in, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the troop of robbers spoileth without. <hi type="super">2</hi> And they consider not in their hearts <hi type="italic">that</hi> I remember all their wickedness: now their own doings have beset them about; they are before my face. <hi type="super">3</hi> They make the king glad with their wickedness, and the princes with their lies. <hi type="super">4</hi> They <hi type="italic">are</hi> all adulterers, as an oven heated by the baker, <hi type="italic">who</hi> ceaseth from raising after he hath kneaded the dough, until it be leavened. <hi type="super">5</hi> In the day of our king the princes have made <hi type="italic">him</hi> sick with bottles of wine; he stretched out his hand with scorners. <hi type="super">6</hi> For they have made ready their heart like an oven, whiles they lie in wait: their baker sleepeth all the night; in the morning it burneth as a flaming fire. <hi type="super">7</hi> They are all hot as an oven, and have devoured their judges; all their kings are fallen: <hi type="italic">there is</hi> none among them that calleth unto me. <div eID="gen19796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19797" type="x-p"/> Some take away the last words of the foregoing chapter, and make them the beginning of this: "<hi type="italic">When I returned,</hi> or <hi type="italic">would have returned, the captivity of my people,</hi> when I was about to come towards them in ways of mercy, even <hi type="italic">when I would have healed Israel, then the iniquity of Ephraim</hi> (the country and common people) <hi type="italic">was discovered, and the wickedness of Samaria,</hi> the court and the chief city." Now, in these verses, we may observe, <div eID="gen19797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19798" type="x-p"/> I. A general idea given of the present state of Israel, <reference osisRef="Hos.7.1-Hos.7.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. See how the case now stood with them. <div eID="gen19798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19799" type="x-p"/> 1. God graciously designed to do well for them: <hi type="italic">I would have healed Israel.</hi> Israel were sick and wounded; their disease was dangerous and malignant, and likely to be fatal, <reference osisRef="Isa.1.6">Isa. i. 6</reference>. But God offered to be their physician, to undertake the cure, and there was balm in Gilead sufficient to recover the health of the daughter of his people; their case was bad, but it was not desperate, nay, it was hopeful, when God <hi type="italic">would have healed Israel.</hi> (1.) He would have reformed them, would have separated between them and their sins, would have purged out the corruptions that were among them, by his laws and prophets. (2.) He would have delivered them out of their troubles, and restored to them their peace and prosperity. Several healing attempts were made, and their declining state seemed sometimes to be in a hopeful way of recovery; but their own folly put them back again. Note, If sinful miserable souls be not healed and helped, but perish in their sin and misery, they cannot lay the blame on God, for he both could and <hi type="italic">would have healed them;</hi> he offered to take the ruin under his hand. And there are some special seasons when God manifests his readiness to heal a distempered church and nation, now and then a hopeful crisis, which, if carefully watched and improved, might, even when the case is very bad, turn the scale for life and health. <div eID="gen19799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19800" type="x-p"/> 2. They stood in their own light and put a bar in their own door. When God <hi type="italic">would have healed them,</hi> when they bade fair for reformation and peace, then their <hi type="italic">iniquity</hi> was <hi type="italic">discovered</hi> and their <hi type="italic">wickedness,</hi> which stopped that current of God's favours, and undid all again. (1.) <hi type="italic">Then,</hi> when their case came to be examined and enquired into, in order to their cure, that wickedness which had been concealed and palliated was <hi type="italic">found out;</hi> not that it was ever hid from God, but he speaks after the manner of men; as a surgeon, when he probes a wound in order to the cure of it and finds that it touches the vitals and is incurable, goes no further in his endeavour to cure it, so, when God <hi type="italic">came down to see</hi> the case of Israel (as the expression is, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.21">Gen. xviii. 21</reference>), with kind intentions towards them, he found their wickedness so very flagrant, and them so hardened in it, so impudent and impenitent, that he could not in honour show them the favour he designed them. Note, Sinners are not healed because they would not be healed. Christ <hi type="italic">would have gathered</hi> them, and they <hi type="italic">would not.</hi> (2.) <hi type="italic">Then,</hi> when some endeavours were used to reform and reclaim them, that wickedness which had been restrained and kept under <hi type="italic">broke out;</hi> and from God's steps towards the healing of them they took occasion to be so much the more provoking. When endeavours were used to reform them vice grew more impetuous, more outrageous, and swelled so much the higher, as a stream when it is damned up. When they began to prosper they grew more proud, wanton, and secure, and so stopped the progress of their cure. Note, It is sin that turns away good things from us when they are coming towards us; and it is the folly and ruin of multitudes that, when God would do well for them, they do ill for themselves. And what was it that did them this mischief? In one word, <hi type="italic">they commit falsehood;</hi> they worship idols (so some), defraud one another (so others), or, rather, they dissemble with God in their professions of repentance and regard to him. They say that they are desirous to be healed by him, and, in order to that, willing to be ruled by him; but they <hi type="italic">lie unto him with their mouth and flatter him with their tongue.</hi> <div eID="gen19800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19801" type="x-p"/> 3. A practical disbelief of God's omniscience and government was at the bottom of all their wickedness (<reference osisRef="Hos.7.2">v. 2</reference>): "<hi type="italic">They consider not in their hearts,</hi> they never say it to their own hearts, never think of this, <hi type="italic">that I remember all their wickedness.</hi>" As if God could not see it, though he is all eye, or did not heed it, though his name is Jealous, or had forgotten it, though he is an eternal mind that can never be unmindful, or would not reckon for it, though he is the <hi type="italic">Judge of heaven and earth.</hi> This is the sinner's atheism; as good say that there is <hi type="italic">no God</hi> as say that he is either ignorant or forgetful, that there is <hi type="italic">none that judges in the earth</hi> as that he remembers not the things he is to give judgment upon. It is a high affront they put upon God; it is a damning cheat they put upon themselves; they say, <hi type="italic">The Lord shall not see,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.94.7">Ps. xciv. 7</reference>. They cannot but know that <hi type="italic">God remembers all their works;</hi> they have been told it many a time; nay, if you ask them, they cannot but own it, and yet they do not <hi type="italic">consider it;</hi> they do not think of it when they should, and with application to themselves and their own works, else they would not, they durst not, do as they do. But the time will come when those who thus deceive themselves shall be undeceived: "<hi type="italic">Now their own doings have beset them about,</hi> that is, they have come at length to such a pitch of wickedness that their sins appear on every side of them; all their neighbours see how bad they are, and can they think that God does not see it?" Or, rather, "The punishment of their doings besets them about; they are surrounded and embarrassed with troubles, so that they cannot get out, by which it appears that the sins they smart for are <hi type="italic">before my face,</hi> not only that I have seen them, but that I am displeased at them;" for, till God by pardoning our sins has cast them behind his back, they are still before his face. Note, Sooner or later, God will convince those who do not now consider it that he <hi type="italic">remembers all their works.</hi> <div eID="gen19801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19802" type="x-p"/> 4. God had begun to contend with them by his judgments, in earnest of what was further coming: <hi type="italic">The thief comes in, and the troop of robbers spoils without.</hi> Some take this as an instance of their wickedness, that they robbed and spoiled one another. <hi type="italic">Nec hospes ab hospite tutus—The host and the guest stand in fear of each other.</hi> It seems rather to be a punishment of their sin; they were infested with secret thieves among themselves, that robbed their houses and shops and picked their pockets, and <hi type="italic">troops of robbers,</hi> foreign invaders, that with open violence <hi type="italic">spoiled abroad;</hi> so far was Israel from being healed that they had fresh wounds given them daily by robbers and spoilers; and all this the effect of sin, all to punish them for robbing God, <reference osisRef="Isa.42.24">Isa. xlii. 24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mal.3.8-Mal.3.11">Mal. iii. 8, 11</reference>. <div eID="gen19802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19803" type="x-p"/> II. A particular account of the sins of the court, of the king and princes, and those about them, and the tokens of God's displeasure that they were under for them. <div eID="gen19803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19804" type="x-p"/> 1. Their king and princes were pleased with the wickedness and profaneness of their subjects, who were emboldened thereby to be so much them ore wicked (<reference osisRef="Hos.7.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">They make the king and princes glad with their wickedness.</hi> It pleased them to see the people conform to their wicked laws and examples, in the worship of their idols, and other instances of impiety and immorality, and to hear them flatter and applaud them in their wicked ways. When Herod saw that his wickedness pleased the people he proceeded further in it, much more will the people do so when they see that it pleases the prince, <reference osisRef="Acts.12.3">Acts xii. 3</reference>. Particularly, they made them glad <hi type="italic">with their lies,</hi> with the lying praises with which they crowned the favourites of the prince and the lying calumnies and censures with which they blackened those whom they knew the princes had a dislike to. Those who show themselves pleased with slanders and ill-natured stories shall never want those about them who will fill their ears with such stories. <reference osisRef="Prov.29.12">Prov. xxix. 12</reference>, <hi type="italic">If a ruler hearken to lies, all his servants are wicked,</hi> and will make him glad with their lies. <div eID="gen19804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19805" type="x-p"/> 2. Drunkenness and revelling abound much at the court, <reference osisRef="Hos.7.5">v. 5</reference>. The <hi type="italic">day of our king</hi> was a merry day with them, either his birth-day or his inauguration-day, of which it is probable that they had an anniversary observation, or perhaps it was some holiday of his appointing, which was therefore called <hi type="italic">his day;</hi> on that day the princes met to drink the king's health, and got him among them, to be merry, and <hi type="italic">made him sick with bottles of wine.</hi> It should seem the king did not ordinarily drink to excess, but he was not upon a high day brought to it by the artifices of the princes, tempted by the goodness of the wine, the gaiety of the company, or the healths they urged; and so little was he used to it that it <hi type="italic">made him sick;</hi> and it is justly charged as a crime, as <hi type="italic">crimen læsæ majestatis—treason,</hi> upon those who thus imposed upon him and <hi type="italic">made him sick;</hi> nor would it serve for an excuse that it was <hi type="italic">the day of their king,</hi> but was rather an aggravation of the crime, that, whey they pretended to do him honour, they dishonoured him to the highest degree. If it is a great affront and injury to a common person to make him drunk, and there is a woe to those that do it (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.15">Hab. ii. 15</reference>), much more to a crowned head; for the greater any man's dignity is the greater disgrace it is to him to be drunk. <hi type="italic">It is not for kings, O Lemuel! it is not for kings, to drink wine,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.31.4-Prov.31.5">Prov. xxxi. 4, 5</reference>. See what a prejudice the sin of drunkenness is to a man, to a king. (1.) In his health; it <hi type="italic">made him sick.</hi> It is a force upon nature; and strange it is by what charms men, otherwise rational enough, can be drawn to that which besides the offence it gives to God, and the damage it does to their spiritual and eternal welfare, is a present disorder and distemper to their own bodies. (2.) In his honour; for, when he was thus intoxicated, he <hi type="italic">stretched out his hand with scorners;</hi> then he that was entrusted with the government of a kingdom lost the government of himself, and so far forgot, [1.] The dignity of a king that he made himself familiar with players and buffoons, and those whose company was a scandal. [2.] The duty of a king that he joined in confederacy with atheists, and the profane scoffers at religion, whom he ought to have silenced and put to shame; he <hi type="italic">sat in the seat of the scornful,</hi> of those that had arrived at the highest pitch of impiety; he struck in with them, said as they said, did as they did, and exerted his power, and <hi type="italic">stretched forth the hand</hi> of his government, in concurrence with them. Goodness and good men are often made <hi type="italic">the song of the drunkards</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.12">Ps. lxix. 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.35.16">xxxv. 16</reference>); but <hi type="italic">woe unto thee, O land!</hi> when <hi type="italic">thy king is such a child</hi> as to <hi type="italic">stretch forth his hand</hi> with those that make them so, <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.16">Eccl. x. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen19805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19806" type="x-p"/> 3. Adultery and uncleanness prevailed much among the courtiers. This is spoken of <reference osisRef="Hos.7.4">v. 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.7.6">6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.7.7">7</reference>, and the charge of drunkenness comes in in the midst of this article; for wine is oil to the fire of lust, <reference osisRef="Prov.23.33">Prov. xxiii. 33</reference>. Those that are inflamed with fleshly lusts, that are <hi type="italic">adulterers</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.7.4">v. 4</reference>), are here again and again compared to an oven heated by the baker (<reference osisRef="Hos.7.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">They have made ready their heart like an oven</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.7.6">v. 6</reference>); <hi type="italic">they are all hot as an oven,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.7.7">v. 7</reference>. Note, (1.) An unclean heart is like an oven heated; and the unclean lusts and affections of it are as the fuel that makes it hot. It is an inward fire, it keeps the heat within itself; so adulterers and fornicators secretly <hi type="italic">burn in lust,</hi> as the expression is, <reference osisRef="Rom.1.27">Rom. i. 27</reference>. The heat of the oven is an intense heat, especially as it is here described; he that heats it <hi type="italic">stirs up</hi> the fire, and <hi type="italic">ceases not from raising</hi> it up, till the bread is ready to be put in, being <hi type="italic">kneaded</hi> and <hi type="italic">leavened,</hi> all which only signifies that they are like an oven when it is at the hottest; nay, when it is <hi type="italic">too hot for the baker</hi> (so the learned Dr. Pocock), when it is <hi type="italic">hotter than he would have it,</hi> so that the raiser up of the fire ceases as long as while the dough that is kneaded is in the fermenting, that the heat may abate a little. Thus fiery hot are the lusts of an unclean heart. (2.) The unclean wait for an opportunity to compass their wicked desires; having made ready their heart like an oven, they lie in wait to catch their prey. <hi type="italic">The eye of the adulterer waits for the twilight,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.24.15">Job xxiv. 15</reference>. <hi type="italic">Their baker sleeps all the night, but in the morning it burns as a flaming fire.</hi> As the baker, having kindled a fire in his oven and laid sufficient fuel to it, goes to bed, and sleeps all night, and in the morning finds his oven well heated, and ready for his purpose, so these wicked people, when they have laid some wicked plot, and formed a design for the gratifying of some covetous, ambitious, revengeful, or unclean lusts, have their hearts so fully set in them to do evil that, though they may stifle them for a while, yet the fire of corrupt affections is still glowing within, and, as soon as ever there is an opportunity for it, their purposes which they have compassed and imagined break out into overt acts, as a fire flames out when it has vent given it. Thus <hi type="italic">they are all hot as an oven.</hi> Note, Lust in the heart is like fire in an oven, puts it into a heat; but the day is coming when those who thus make themselves like a fiery oven with their own vile affections, if that fire be not extinguished by divine grace, shall be made as a fiery oven by divine wrath (<reference osisRef="Ps.21.9">Ps. xxi. 9</reference>), when <hi type="italic">the day comes</hi> that shall <hi type="italic">burn as an oven,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.4.1">Mal. iv. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen19806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19807" type="x-p"/> 4. They resist the proper methods of reformation and redress: <hi type="italic">They have devoured their judges,</hi> those few good judges that were among them, that would have put out these fires with which they were heated; they fell foul upon them, and would not suffer them to do justice, but were ready to stone them, and perhaps did so; or, as some think, they provoked God to deprive them of the blessing of magistracy and to leave all in confusion: <hi type="italic">All their kings</hi> have <hi type="italic">fallen</hi> one after another, and their families with them, which could not but put the kingdom into confusion, crumble it into contending parties, and occasion a great deal of bloodshed. There are heart-burnings among them; they are <hi type="italic">hot as an oven</hi> with rage and malice at one another, and this occasions the <hi type="italic">devouring of their judges,</hi> the <hi type="italic">falling</hi> of their <hi type="italic">kings. For the transgressions of a land many are the princes thereof,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.28.2">Prov. xxviii. 2</reference>. But in the midst of all this trouble and disorder <hi type="italic">there is none among them that calls unto God,</hi> that sees his hand stretched out against them in these judgments, and deprecates the strokes of it, none, or next to none, that stir up themselves to take hold on God, <reference osisRef="Isa.64.7">Isa. lxiv. 7</reference>. Note, Those are not only heated with sin, but hardened in sin, that continue to live without prayer even when they are in trouble and distress.
entries.7ec5676804cb2a074149298498e7e7b470f02bdd: <div eID="gen19807" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Crimes of the People; Infatuation of Ephraim; Ephraim's Obstinate Rebellion; Ephraim's Hypocrisy. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi>  750.)</title> <div sID="gen19808" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Ephraim, he hath mixed himself among the people; Ephraim is a cake not turned. <hi type="super">9</hi> Strangers have devoured his strength, and he knoweth <hi type="italic">it</hi> not: yea, gray hairs are here and there upon him, yet he knoweth not. <hi type="super">10</hi> And the pride of Israel testifieth to his face: and they do not return to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> their God, nor seek him for all this. <hi type="super">11</hi> Ephraim also is like a silly dove without heart: they call to Egypt, they go to Assyria. <hi type="super">12</hi> When they shall go, I will spread my net upon them; I will bring them down as the fowls of the heaven; I will chastise them, as their congregation hath heard. <hi type="super">13</hi> Woe unto them! for they have fled from me: destruction unto them! because they have transgressed against me: though I have redeemed them, yet they have spoken lies against me. <hi type="super">14</hi> And they have not cried unto me with their heart, when they howled upon their beds: they assemble themselves for corn and wine, <hi type="italic">and</hi> they rebel against me. <hi type="super">15</hi> Though I have bound <hi type="italic">and</hi> strengthened their arms, yet do they imagine mischief against me. <hi type="super">16</hi> They return, <hi type="italic">but</hi> not to the most High: they are like a deceitful bow: their princes shall fall by the sword for the rage of their tongue: this <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> their derision in the land of Egypt. <div eID="gen19808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19809" type="x-p"/> Having seen how vicious and corrupt the court was, we now come to enquire how it is with the country, and we find that to be no better; and no marvel if the distemper that has so seized the head affect the whole body, so that there is <hi type="italic">no soundness</hi> in it; the <hi type="italic">iniquity of Ephraim is discovered,</hi> as well as <hi type="italic">the sin of Samaria,</hi> of the people as well as the princes, of which here are divers instances. <div eID="gen19809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19810" type="x-p"/> I. They were not peculiar and entire for God, as they should have been, <reference osisRef="Hos.7.8">v. 8</reference>. 1. They did not distinguish themselves from the heathen, as God had distinguished them: <hi type="italic">Ephraim, he has mingled himself among the people,</hi> has associated with them, and conformed himself to them, and has in a manner confounded himself with them and lost his character among them. God had said, <hi type="italic">The people shall dwell alone;</hi> but they <hi type="italic">mingled themselves with the heathen and learned their works,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.16.35">Ps. xvi. 35</reference>. They went up and down among the heathen, to beg help of one of them against another (so some); whereas, if they had kept close to God, they would not have needed the help of any of them. 2. They were not entirely devoted to God: <hi type="italic">Ephraim is a cake not turned,</hi> and so is burnt on one side and dough on the other side, but good for nothing on either side. As in Ahab's time, so now, they <hi type="italic">halted between God and Baal;</hi> sometimes they seemed zealous for God, but at other times as hot for Baal. Note, It is sad to think how many, who, after a sort, profess religion, are made up of contraries and inconsistencies, <hi type="italic">as a cake not turned,</hi> a constant self-contradiction, and always in one extreme or the other. <div eID="gen19810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19811" type="x-p"/> II. They were strangely insensible of the judgments of God, which they were under, and which threatened their ruin, <reference osisRef="Hos.7.9">v. 9</reference>. Observe, 1. The condition they were in. God was not to them, in his judgments, as <hi type="italic">a moth</hi> and as <hi type="italic">rottenness;</hi> they were silently and slowly drawing towards the ruin of their state partly by the encroachments of foreigners upon them: <hi type="italic">Strangers have devoured his strength,</hi> and eaten him up; they have wasted his wealth and treasure, lessened his numbers, and consumed the fruits of the earth. Some devoured them by open wars (as <reference osisRef="2Kgs.13.7">2 Kings xiii. 7</reference>, when the king of Syria made them <hi type="italic">like the dust by threshing</hi>), others by pretending treaties of peace and amity, in which they extorted abundance of wealth from them, and made them pay dearly for that which did them no good, but which afterwards they paid more dearly for, as <reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.9">2 Kings xvi. 9</reference>. This Ephraim got by mingling with the heathen, and suffering them to mingle with him; they devoured that which he rested upon and supported himself with. Note, Those that make not God their strength (<reference osisRef="Ps.52.7">Ps. lii. 7</reference>) make that their strength which will soon be devoured by strangers. They were thus reduced partly by their own mal-administrations among themselves: <hi type="italic">Yea, gray hairs are here and there upon him</hi> (are <hi type="italic">sprinkled</hi> upon him, so the word is), that is, the sad symptoms of a decaying declining state, which is <hi type="italic">waxing old</hi> and <hi type="italic">ready to vanish away,</hi> and the effects of trouble and vexation. <hi type="italic">Cura facit canos—Care turns gray.</hi> The <hi type="italic">almond-tree</hi> does not as yet <hi type="italic">flourish,</hi> but it begins to turn colour, which speaks aloud to him that the <hi type="italic">evil days</hi> are coming, and the <hi type="italic">years of which he shall say, I have no pleasure in them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.1">Eccl. xii. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.5">5</reference>. 2. Their regardlessness of these warnings: <hi type="italic">He knows it not;</hi> he is not aware of the hand of God gone out against him; it is lifted up, but he <hi type="italic">will not see,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.26.11">Isa. xxvi. 11</reference>. He does not know how near his ruin is, and takes no care to prevent it. Note, Stupidity under less judgments is a presage of greater coming. <div eID="gen19811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19812" type="x-p"/> III. They went on frowardly in their wicked ways, and were not reclaimed by the rebukes they were under (<reference osisRef="Hos.7.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">The pride of Israel</hi> still <hi type="italic">testifies to his face,</hi> as it had done before (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.5">ch. v. 5</reference>); under humbling providences their hearts were still unhumbled, their lusts unmortified; and it is <hi type="italic">through the pride of their countenance</hi> that they <hi type="italic">will not seek after God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.4">Ps. x. 4</reference>); they <hi type="italic">do not return to the Lord their God</hi> by repentance and reformation, <hi type="italic">nor do they seek him</hi> by faith and prayer <hi type="italic">for all this;</hi> though they suffer for going astray from him, though it can never be well with them till they come back to him, and though they have in vain sought to others for relief, yet they think not of applying to God. <div eID="gen19812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19813" type="x-p"/> IV. They were infatuated in their counsels, and took very wrong methods when they were in distress (<reference osisRef="Hos.7.11-Hos.7.12">v. 11, 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">Ephraim is like a silly dove without heart.</hi> To be harmless as a dove, without gall, and not to hurt or injure others, is commendable; but to be sottish as a dove, without heart, that knows not how to defend herself and provide for her own safety, is a shame. <div eID="gen19813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19814" type="x-p"/> 1. The silliness of this dove is, (1.) That she laments not the loss of her young that are taken from her, but will make her nest again in the same place; so they have their people carried away by the enemy, and are not affected with it, but continue their dealings with those that deal barbarously with them. (2.) That she is easily enticed by the bait into the net, and has <hi type="italic">no heart,</hi> no understanding, to discern her danger, as many other fowls do, <reference osisRef="Prov.1.17">Prov. i. 17</reference>. She <hi type="italic">hastes to the snare, and knows not that it is for her life</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.7.23">Prov. vii. 23</reference>); so they were drawn into leagues with neighbouring nations that were their ruin. (3.) That, when she is frightened, she has not courage to stay in the dove-house, where she is safe, and under the careful protection of her owner, but flutters and hovers, seeking shelter first in one place, then in another, and thereby exposes herself so much the more; so this people, when they were in distress, sought not to God, did not fly <hi type="italic">like the doves to their windows</hi> where they might have been secured from all the birds of prey that struck at them, but threw themselves out of God's protection, and then <hi type="italic">called to Egypt</hi> to help them, and went in all haste <hi type="italic">to Assyria,</hi> to seek for that aid in vain which they might, by repentance and prayer, have found nearer home, in their God. Note, It is a silly senseless thing for those who have a God in heaven to trust to creatures for the refuge and relief which are to be had in him only; and those that do so are a <hi type="italic">people of no understanding,</hi> they are <hi type="italic">without heart.</hi> Now, <div eID="gen19814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19815" type="x-p"/> 2. See what becomes of this <hi type="italic">silly dove</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.7.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">When they shall go</hi> to Egypt and Assyria, <hi type="italic">I will spread my net upon them.</hi> Note, Those that will not abide by the mercy of God must expect to be pursued by the justice of God. Here, (1.) They are ensnared: "<hi type="italic">I will spread my net upon them,</hi> bring them into straits, that they may see their folly and think of returning." Note, It is common for those that go away from God to find snares where they expected shelters. (2.) They are humbled; they soar upward, proud of their foreign alliances and confiding in them; but <hi type="italic">I will bring them down,</hi> let them fly ever so high, <hi type="italic">as the fowls of heaven,</hi> that are shot flying. Note, God can and will <hi type="italic">bring those down</hi> that <hi type="italic">exalt themselves as the eagle,</hi> <reference osisRef="Obad.1.3-Obad.1.4">Obad. 3, 4</reference>. (3.) They are made to smart for their folly: <hi type="italic">I will chastise them.</hi> Note, The disappointments we meet with in the creature, when we put a confidence in it, are a necessary chastisement, or discipline, that we may learn to be wiser another time. (4.) In all this the scripture is fulfilled. It is <hi type="italic">as their congregation has heard;</hi> they have been many a time told by the word of God, read, and preached, and sung, in their religious assemblies, that "<hi type="italic">vain is the help of man,</hi> that <hi type="italic">in the son of man there is no help;</hi> they have heard both from the law and from the prophets what judgments God would bring upon them for their wickedness; and <hi type="italic">as they have heard</hi> now <hi type="italic">they shall see,</hi> they shall feel." Note, It concerns us to take notice of the word of God which we hear from time to time <hi type="italic">in the congregation,</hi> and to be governed by it, for we must shortly be judged by it; and it will justify God in the condemnation of sinners, and aggravate it to them, that they have had plain public warning given them of it; it is what their congregation has heard many a time, but they would not take warning. "<hi type="italic">Son, remember</hi> thou wast told what would come of it; and now thou seest they were not vain words." See <reference osisRef="Zech.1.6">Zech. i. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen19815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19816" type="x-p"/> V. They revolted from God and rebelled against him, notwithstanding the various methods he took to retain them in their allegiance, <reference osisRef="Hos.7.13-Hos.7.15">v. 13-15</reference>. Here observe, <div eID="gen19816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19817" type="x-p"/> 1. How kindly and tenderly God had dealt with them, as a gracious sovereign towards a people dear unto him, and whose prosperity he had much at heart. He had <hi type="italic">redeemed them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.7.13">v. 13</reference>), brought them, at first, out of the land of Egypt, and, since, delivered them out of many a distress. He had <hi type="italic">bound and strengthened their arms,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.7.15">v. 15</reference>. When their power was weakened, like an arm broken or out of joint, God set it again, and bound it, as a surgeon does a broken bone, to make it knit. God had given Israel victories over the Syrians (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.13.16-2Kgs.13.17">2 Kings xiii. 16, 17</reference>), had <hi type="italic">restored their coast</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.25-2Kgs.14.26">2 Kings xiv. 25, 26</reference>), had <hi type="italic">girded them with strength for battle.</hi> "Though <hi type="italic">I have chastened</hi> them" (so the margin reads it), "sometimes corrected them for their faults and thereby taught them, at other times <hi type="italic">strengthened their arms</hi> and relieved them, though I have used both fair means and foul to work upon them, it was all to no purpose; they were mercy-proof and judgment-proof." <div eID="gen19817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19818" type="x-p"/> 2. How impudent their conduct had been towards him notwithstanding, which is described here for the conviction and humiliation of all those who have gone on in any way of wickedness, that they may see how exceedingly sinful their sin is, how heinous, how the God of heaven interprets it, how he resents it. (1.) He had courted them to him, and taken them into covenant with himself; but <hi type="italic">they fled from him,</hi> as if he had been their dangerous enemy who had always approved himself their faithful friend. They wandered from him, as the silly dove from her nest, for those who forsake God will find no rest nor settlement in the creature, but wander endlessly. They fled from God when they forsook the worship of him, and ran away from his service, and withdrew themselves from their allegiance to him. (2.) He had given them his laws, which were all holy, just, and good, by which he designed to keep them in the right way; but they <hi type="italic">transgressed against him;</hi> they sinned with a high hand and a stiff neck, wilfully and presumptuously (so the words signifies); they broke through the fence of the divine law, and therein thwarted the design of the divine love. (3.) He had made known his truths to them, and given them all possible proofs of the sincerity of his good-will to them; and yet they <hi type="italic">spoke lies against him.</hi> They set up false gods in competition with him; they denied his providence and power; thus they <hi type="italic">belied the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.5.12">Jer. v. 12</reference>. They rejected his messages sent them by his prophets, and said that they should have peace, though they went on in sin, directly against what he said. In their hypocritical professions of religion, shows of devotion, and promises of amendment, they lied to the Lord, which he took as lying against him. (4.) He was their rightful Lord and King, and had always ruled in Jacob with equity, and for the public good; and yet they <hi type="italic">rebelled against him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.7.14">v. 14</reference>. They not only went off from him, but took up arms against him, would have deposed him if they could and set up another. (5.) He designed well for them, but they <hi type="italic">imagined mischief against him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.7.15">v. 15</reference>. Sin is a mischievous thing; it is mischief against God, for it is treason against his crown and dignity; not that the sinners can do any thing to hurt their Creator (as one of the ancients observes on these words), but <hi type="italic">what they can they do;</hi> and it is so much the worse when it is not done by surprise, or through inadvertency, but designedly and with contrivance. The Jews have a saying, which Dr. Pocock quotes here, <hi type="italic">The thoughts of transgression are worse than the transgression.</hi> The designing of mischief is doing it, in God's account. <hi type="italic">Compassing and imagining</hi> the death of the king is treason by our law. Those that imagine an evil thing, though it prove a vain thing (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.1">Ps. ii. 1</reference>), will be reckoned with for the imagination. <div eID="gen19818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19819" type="x-p"/> 3. How they shall be punished for this (<reference osisRef="Hos.7.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">Woe unto them! for they have fled from me.</hi> Note, Those who flee from God have woes sent after them, and are, without doubt, in a woeful case. The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against them; the word of God says, <hi type="italic">Woe to them!</hi> And observe what follows immediately, <hi type="italic">Destruction unto them!</hi> Note, The woes of God's word have real effects; destruction makes them good. The judgments of his hand shall verify the judgments of his mouth. Those whom he curses, and pronounces woeful, they are cursed, they are woeful indeed. <div eID="gen19819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19820" type="x-p"/> VI. Their shows of devotion and reformation were but shows, and in them they did but mock God. <div eID="gen19820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19821" type="x-p"/> 1. They pretended devotion, but it was not sincere, <reference osisRef="Hos.7.14">v. 14</reference>. When the hand of God had gone forth against them they made some sort of application to him. <hi type="italic">When he slew them, then they sought him. Lord, in trouble have they visited thee.</hi> But it was all in hypocrisy. (1.) When they were under personal troubles, and called upon God in secret, they were not sincere in that: <hi type="italic">They have not cried unto me with their heart, when they howled upon their beds.</hi> When they were <hi type="italic">chastened with pain upon their beds,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">multitude of their bones with strong pains,</hi> perhaps ill of the wounds they received in war, they cried, and groaned, and complained in the forms of devotion, and, it may be, they used many good words, proper enough for the circumstances they were in; they cried, <hi type="italic">God help us,</hi> and, <hi type="italic">Lord, look upon us.</hi> But they did not <hi type="italic">cry with their heart,</hi> and therefore God reckons it as no crying to him. Moses is said to <hi type="italic">cry unto God</hi> when he spoke not a word, only his heart prayed with faith and fervency, <reference osisRef="Exod.14.15">Exod. xiv. 15</reference>. These made a great noise, and said a great deal, and yet did not <hi type="italic">cry to God,</hi> because their hearts were not <hi type="italic">right with him,</hi> not subjected to his will, devoted to his honour, nor employed in his service. To pray is to <hi type="italic">lift up the soul</hi> to God, this is the essence of prayer. If this be not done, <hi type="italic">words,</hi> though ever so well chosen, <hi type="italic">are but wind;</hi> but, if it be, it is an acceptable prayer, though the <hi type="italic">groanings cannot be uttered.</hi> Note, Those do not pray to God at all that do not pray <hi type="italic">in the spirit.</hi> Nay, God is so far from approving their prayer and accepting it that he calls it <hi type="italic">howling.</hi> Some think it intimates the <hi type="italic">noisiness</hi> of their prayers (they cried to God as they used to cry to Baal, when they thought he must be awakened), or the brutish violent passions which they vented in their prayers; they snarled at the stone, and howled under the whip, but regarded not the hand. Or it denotes that their hypocritical prayers were so far from being pleasing to God that they were offensive to him; he <hi type="italic">was angry at their prayers.</hi> The <hi type="italic">songs of the temple shall be howlings,</hi> <reference osisRef="Amos.8.3">Amos viii. 3</reference>. God will be so far from pitying them that he will justly <hi type="italic">laugh at their calamity,</hi> who have so often laughed at his authority. (2.) When they were under public troubles, and met together to implore God's favour, in that also they were hypocritical; they <hi type="italic">assembled themselves,</hi> for fashion-sake, because it was usual to <hi type="italic">call a solemn assembly</hi> in times of general mourning, <reference osisRef="Zeph.2.1">Zeph. ii. 1</reference>. But it was only to pray <hi type="italic">for corn and wine</hi> that they came together, which were the things they wanted, and feared being deprived of by the want of rain, the judgment they now laboured under. They did not pray for the favour or grace of God, that God would give them repentance, pardon their sins, and turn away his wrath, but only that he would not take away from them <hi type="italic">their corn and wine.</hi> Note, Carnal hearts, in their prayers to God, covet temporal mercies only, and dread and deprecate no other but temporal judgments, for they have no sense of any other. <div eID="gen19821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19822" type="x-p"/> 2. They pretended reformation, but neither was that sincere, <reference osisRef="Hos.7.16">v. 16</reference>. Here is, (1.) The sin of Israel: <hi type="italic">They return,</hi> that is, they make as if they would return; they pretend to repent and amend their doings, but they make nothing of it; they do not come home to God nor return to their allegiance, whereas God says (<reference osisRef="Jer.4.1">Jer. iv. 1</reference>), <hi type="italic">If thou wilt return, O Israel! return to me;</hi> do not only <hi type="italic">turn towards me,</hi> but <hi type="italic">return to me.</hi> This dissimulation of theirs makes them like a <hi type="italic">deceitful bow,</hi> which looks as if it were fit for business, and is bent and drawn accordingly, but, when strength comes to be laid to it, either the bow or the string breaks, and the arrow, instead of flying to the mark, drops at the archer's foot. Such were their essays towards repentance and reformation. (2.) The sin of the princes of Israel. That which is charged upon them is <hi type="italic">the rage of their tongue,</hi> quarrelling with God and his providence and with all about them when they are crossed. Princes think they may say what they will, and that it is their prerogative to huff and bluster, to curse and rail, and to call names at their pleasure, but let them know there is a God above them that will call them to an account for the <hi type="italic">rage of their tongues</hi> and make <hi type="italic">their own tongues to fall upon them.</hi> (3.) The punishment of Israel and their princes for their sin. As for the princes, they shall <hi type="italic">fall by the sword</hi> either of their enemies or of their own people, some by one and some by the other; and <hi type="italic">this shall be their derision,</hi> this is that for which they shall be derided <hi type="italic">in the land of Egypt,</hi> when they flee to the Egyptians for succour, <reference osisRef="Hos.7.11">v. 11</reference>. Their sin and punishment shall make them a laughing-stock to all about them. Note, Those that are treacherous and deceitful in their dealings with God, and passionate and outrageous in their conduct towards men, will justly be made a derision to their neighbours, for they make themselves ridiculous.  <chapter eID="Hos.7"/> <div eID="gen19822" type="x-p"/>

entries.72679028cb4f93b778ba74528f0402425d53ff68: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12322"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 7</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Hos.7.1-Hos.7.16">Ho 7:1-16</reference>. Reproof of Israel.</title> <div sID="gen22492" type="x-p"/> Probably delivered in the interreign and civil war at Pekah's death; for <reference osisRef="Hos.7.7">Ho 7:7</reference>, "all their kings ... fallen," refers to the murder of Zechariah, Shallum, Menahem, Pekahiah, and Pekah. In <reference osisRef="Hos.7.8">Ho 7:8</reference> the reference seems to be to Menahem's payment of tribute to Pul, in order to secure himself in the usurped throne, also to Pekah's league with Rezin of Syria, and to Hoshea's connection with Assyria during the interregnum at Pekah's death [Maurer].<div eID="gen22492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22493" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12322"/><hi type="bold">1. I would have healed Israel--</hi>Israel's restoration of the two hundred thousand Jewish captives at God's command (<reference osisRef="2Chr.28.8-2Chr.28.15">2Ch 28:8-15</reference>) gave hope of Israel's reformation [Henderson]. Political, as well as moral, healing is meant. When I would have healed Israel in its calamitous state, then their iniquity was discovered to be so great as to preclude hope of recovery. Then he enumerates their wickedness: "The thief cometh in (indoors stealthily), and the troop of robbers spoileth without" (out-of-doors with open violence). <div eID="gen22493" type="x-p"/>
entries.03f10cdac302fa8238272becf283b045fc0ec9d0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12323"/><div sID="gen22494" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12323"/><hi type="bold">2. consider not in their hearts--</hi>literally, "say not to," &c. (<reference osisRef="Ps.14.1">Psa 14:1</reference>).<div eID="gen22494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22495" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that I remember--</hi>and will punish.<div eID="gen22495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22496" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their own doings have beset them about--</hi>as so many witnesses against them (<reference osisRef="Ps.9.16">Psa 9:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.5.22">Pr 5:22</reference>).<div eID="gen22496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22497" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">before my face--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.90.8">Psa 90:8</reference>). <div eID="gen22497" type="x-p"/>
entries.0d6d71d2806954967df4c2889276aaee1fc6baf0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12324"/><div sID="gen22498" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12324"/>3. Their princes, instead of checking, "have pleasure in them that do" such crimes (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.32">Ro 1:32</reference>). <div eID="gen22498" type="x-p"/>
entries.06061eabb8f46584c6183200049fa6fde4db3c07: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12325"/><div sID="gen22499" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12325"/><hi type="bold">4. who ceaseth from raising--</hi>rather, "heating" it, from an Arabic root, "to be hot." So the Septuagint. Their adulterous and idolatrous lust is inflamed as the oven of a baker who has it at such a heat that he ceaseth from heating it only from the time that he hath kneaded the dough, until it be leavened; he only needs to omit feeding it during the short period of the fermentation of the bread. Compare <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.14">2Pe 2:14</reference>, "that cannot cease from sin" [Henderson]. <div eID="gen22499" type="x-p"/>
entries.4763dfbc5b29cbe66509969bbb4a113d59f75a9c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12326"/><div sID="gen22500" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12326"/><hi type="bold">5. the day of our king--</hi>his birthday or day of inauguration.<div eID="gen22500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22501" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">have made him sick--</hi>namely, the king. Maurer translates, "make themselves sick."<div eID="gen22501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22502" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with bottles of wine--</hi>drinking not merely glasses, but bottles. Maurer translates, "Owing to the heat of wine."<div eID="gen22502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22503" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he stretched out his hand with scorners--</hi>the gesture of revellers in holding out the cup and in drinking to one another's health. Scoffers were the king's boon companions. <div eID="gen22503" type="x-p"/>
entries.0f481372404723ce800fda3b8fad4ccbd23d2b16: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12327"/><div sID="gen22504" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12327"/><hi type="bold">6. they have made ready--</hi>rather, "they make their heart approach," namely their king, in going to drink with him.<div eID="gen22504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22505" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">like an oven--</hi>following out the image in <reference osisRef="Hos.7.4">Ho 7:4</reference>. As it conceals the lighted fire all night while the baker sleeps but in the morning burns as a flaming fire, so they brood mischief in their hearts while conscience is lulled asleep, and their wicked designs wait only for a fair occasion to break forth [Horsley]. Their heart is the oven, their baker the ringleader of the plot. In <reference osisRef="Hos.7.7">Ho 7:7</reference> their plots appear, namely, the intestine disturbances and murders of one king after another, after Jeroboam II. <div eID="gen22505" type="x-p"/>
entries.4a2088184311816ad8eb8d49a34a45617722f5e4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12328"/><div sID="gen22506" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12328"/><hi type="bold">7. all hot--</hi>All burn with eagerness to cause universal disturbance (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.1-2Kgs.15.38">2Ki 15:1-38</reference>).<div eID="gen22506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22507" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">devoured their judges--</hi>magistrates; as the fire of the oven devours the fuel.<div eID="gen22507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22508" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all their kings ... fallen--</hi>See on <reference osisRef="Hos.7.1">Ho 7:1</reference>.<div eID="gen22508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22509" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">none ... calleth unto me--</hi>Such is their perversity that amid all these national calamities, none seeks help from Me (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.13">Is 9:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.64.7">64:7</reference>). <div eID="gen22509" type="x-p"/>
entries.95c3a8fa250be0cb8d311ff5bd78d44526dc9ac3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12329"/><div sID="gen22510" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12329"/><hi type="bold">8. mixed ... among the people--</hi>by leagues with idolaters, and the adoption of their idolatrous practices (<reference osisRef="Hos.7.9">Ho 7:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.7.11">11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.106.35">Psa 106:35</reference>).<div eID="gen22510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22511" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Ephraim ... cake not turned--</hi>a cake burnt on one side and unbaked on the other, and so uneatable; an image of the worthlessness of Ephraim. The Easterners bake their bread on the ground, covering it with embers (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.6">1Ki 19:6</reference>), and turning it every ten minutes, to bake it thoroughly without burning it. <div eID="gen22511" type="x-p"/>
entries.161be53819dc944b70a1f31ebdf36be68f358701: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12330"/><div sID="gen22512" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12330"/><hi type="bold">9. Strangers--</hi>foreigners: the Syrians and Assyrians (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.13.7">2Ki 13:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.19">15:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.20">20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.3-2Kgs.17.6">17:3-6</reference>).<div eID="gen22512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22513" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gray hairs--</hi>that is, symptoms of approaching national dissolution.<div eID="gen22513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22514" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">are here and there upon--</hi>literally, "are sprinkled on" him.<div eID="gen22514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22515" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">yet he knoweth not--</hi>Though old age ought to bring with it wisdom, he neither knows of his senile decay, nor has the true knowledge which leads to reformation. <div eID="gen22515" type="x-p"/>
entries.0187773f2f3a708736db2a28ce32caf67ceb598e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12331"/><div sID="gen22516" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12331"/>10. Repetition of <reference osisRef="Hos.5.5">Ho 5:5</reference>.<div eID="gen22516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22517" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not return to ... Lord ... for all this--</hi>notwithstanding all their calamities (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.13">Is 9:13</reference>). <div eID="gen22517" type="x-p"/>
entries.5d253aad384de223669f0fb71e2aaa9a864b0b85: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12332"/><div sID="gen22518" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12332"/><hi type="bold">11. like a silly dove--</hi>a bird proverbial for simplicity: easily deceived.<div eID="gen22518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22519" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">without heart--</hi>that is, understanding.<div eID="gen22519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22520" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">call to Egypt--</hi>Israel lying between the two great rival empires Egypt and Assyria, sought each by turns to help her against the other. As this prophecy was written in the reign of Hoshea, the allusion is probably to the alliance with So or Sabacho II (of which a record has been found on the clay cylindrical seals in Koyunjik), which ended in the overthrow of Hoshea and the deportation of Israel (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.3-2Kgs.17.6">2Ki 17:3-6</reference>). As the dove betrays its foolishness by fleeing in alarm from its nest only to fall into the net of the fowler, so Israel, though warned that foreign alliances would be their ruin, rushed into them. <div eID="gen22520" type="x-p"/>
entries.1835336802f33d7f615db3143c858be8230da578: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12333"/><div sID="gen22521" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12333"/><hi type="bold">12. When they shall go--</hi>to seek aid from this or that foreign state.<div eID="gen22521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22522" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">spread my net upon them--</hi>as on birds taken on the ground (<reference osisRef="Ezek.12.13">Eze 12:13</reference>), as contrasted with "bringing them down" as the "fowls of the heavens," namely, by the use of missiles.<div eID="gen22522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22523" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as their congregation hath heard--</hi>namely, by My prophets through whom I threatened "chastisement" (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.9">Ho 5:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.13-2Kgs.17.18">2Ki 17:13-18</reference>). <div eID="gen22523" type="x-p"/>
entries.d0b6c28e3ff70270e1155d795283a80338327a18: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12334"/><div sID="gen22524" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12334"/><hi type="bold">13. fled--</hi>as birds from their nest (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.8">Pr 27:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.16.2">Is 16:2</reference>).<div eID="gen22524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22525" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">me--</hi>who both could and would have healed them (<reference osisRef="Hos.7.1">Ho 7:1</reference>), had they applied to Me.<div eID="gen22525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22526" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">redeemed them--</hi>from Egypt and their other enemies (<reference osisRef="Mic.6.4">Mi 6:4</reference>).<div eID="gen22526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22527" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lies--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.78.36">Psa 78:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.10">Jr 3:10</reference>). Pretending to be My worshippers, when they all the while worshipped idols (<reference osisRef="Hos.7.14">Ho 7:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.12.1">Ho 12:1</reference>); also defrauding Me of the glory of their deliverance, and ascribing it and their other blessings to idols [Calvin]. <div eID="gen22527" type="x-p"/>
entries.ae62c7f43bac7add60b66e5110d663f720f31a7c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12335"/><div sID="gen22528" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12335"/><hi type="bold">14. not cried unto me--</hi>but unto other gods [Maurer], (<reference osisRef="Job.35.9">Job 35:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.35.10">10</reference>). Or, they did indeed cry unto Me, but not "with their heart": answering to "lies," <reference osisRef="Hos.7.13">Ho 7:13</reference> (see on <reference osisRef="Hos.7.13">Ho 7:13</reference>).<div eID="gen22528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22529" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when they howled upon their beds--</hi>sleepless with anxiety; image of deep affliction. Their cry is termed "howling," as it is the cry of anguish, not the cry of repentance and faith.<div eID="gen22529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22530" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">assemble ... for corn, &c.--</hi>namely in the temples of their idols, to obtain from them a good harvest and vintage, instead of coming to Me, the true Giver of these (<reference osisRef="Hos.2.5">Ho 2:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.12">8, 12</reference>), proving that their cry to God was "not with their heart."<div eID="gen22530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22531" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rebel against me--</hi>literally, "withdraw themselves against Me," that is, not only withdraw from Me, but also rebel against Me. <div eID="gen22531" type="x-p"/>
entries.fe96149905af539516c9ee75b49c25a837f4de2e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12336"/><div sID="gen22532" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12336"/><hi type="bold">15. I ... bound--</hi>when I saw their arms as it were relaxed with various disasters, I bound them so as to strengthen their sinews; image from surgery [Calvin]. Maurer translates, "I instructed them" to war (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.34">Psa 18:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.144.1">144:1</reference>), namely, under Jeroboam II (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.25">2Ki 14:25</reference>). Grotius explains, "Whether I chastised them (Margin) or strengthened their arms, they imagined mischief against Me." English Version is best. <div eID="gen22532" type="x-p"/>
entries.f5c93bd6bbe573563a897abbe0ef52b914c37a73: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12337"/><div sID="gen22533" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12337"/><hi type="bold">16. return, but not to the Most High--</hi>or, "to one who is not the Most High," one very different from Him, a stock or a stone. So the Septuagint.<div eID="gen22533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22534" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">deceitful bow--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.78.57">Psa 78:57</reference>). A bow which, from its faulty construction, shoots wide of the mark. So Israel pretends to seek God, but turns aside to idols.<div eID="gen22534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22535" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for the rage of their tongue--</hi>their boast of safety from Egyptian aid, and their "lies" (<reference osisRef="Hos.7.13">Ho 7:13</reference>), whereby they pretended to serve God, while worshipping idols; also their perverse defense for their idolatries and blasphemies against God and His prophets (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.9">Psa 73:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.120.2">120:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.120.3">3</reference>).<div eID="gen22535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22536" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their derision in ... Egypt--</hi>Their "fall" shall be the subject of "derision" to Egypt, to whom they had applied for help (<reference osisRef="Hos.9.3">Ho 9:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.9.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.4">2Ki 17:4</reference>). <chapter eID="Hos.7"/>

entries.ca64cc7fcd27e259d8704b8d469c2458166807b6: <div eID="gen33707" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen33708" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33709" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33709" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33708" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33710" type="x-p"/> Here God complains that though he had employed every means for reforming Israel, they still persisted in their iniquity, without fearing the consequences, <reference osisRef="Hos.7.1">Hos 7:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.7.2">Hos 7:2</reference>; that those who ought to check their crimes were pleased with them, <reference osisRef="Hos.7.3">Hos 7:3</reference>; and that they all burned with adultery, as an oven when fully heated, and ready to receive the kneaded dough, <reference osisRef="Hos.7.4">Hos 7:4</reference>. The fifth verse alludes to some recent enormities; the sixth charges them with dividing their time between inactivity and iniquity; the seventh alludes to their civil broils and conspiracies; (see <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.10">2Kgs 15:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.14">2Kgs 15:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.25">2Kgs 15:25</reference>); the eighth to their joining themselves with idolatrous nations; and the ninth describes the sad consequence. The tenth verse reproves their pride and open contempt of God's worship; the eleventh reproves their foolish conduct in applying for aid to their enemies; (see <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.19">2Kgs 15:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.4">2Kgs 17:4</reference>); the twelfth and thirteenth threaten them with punishments; the fourteenth charges them with hypocrisy in their acts of humiliation; the fifteenth with ingratitude; and the image of the deceitful bow, in the sixteenth verse, is highly expressive of their frequent apostasies; and their hard speeches against God shall be visited upon them by their becoming a reproach in the land of their enemies. <div eID="gen33710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33711" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen33711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33712" type="x-p"/> When I would have healed Israel - As soon as one wound was healed, another was discovered. Scarcely was one sin blotted out till another was committed. <div eID="gen33712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33713" type="x-p"/> The thief cometh in - Their own princes spoil them. <div eID="gen33713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33714" type="x-p"/> The troop of robbers spoileth without - The Assyrians, under different leaders, waste and plunder the country.
entries.6fb9f53f8278412ae8d5c5f44d5c3e7d7fa7e634: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen33714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33715" type="x-p"/> They consider not in their hearts - They do not consider that my eye is upon all their ways; they do not think that I record all their wickedness; and they know not their own evil doings are as a host of enemies encompassing them about.
entries.58fd197200ed4887bb75f8f2e4ae1f2f298ac6be: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen33715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33716" type="x-p"/> They make the king glad - They pleased Jeroboam by coming readily into his measures, and heartily joining with him in his idolatry. And they professed to be perfectly happy in their change, and to be greatly advantaged by their new gods; and that the religion of the state now was better than that of Jehovah. Thus, they made all their rulers, "glad with their lies."
entries.25f517cd2312b03effe16b9065e0e15d20fc2207: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen33716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33717" type="x-p"/> As an oven heated by the baker - Calmet's paraphrase on this and the following verses expresses pretty nearly the sense: Hosea makes a twofold comparison of the Israelites; to an oven, and to dough. Jeroboam set fire to his own oven - his kingdom - and put the leaven in his dough; and afterwards went to rest, that the fire might have time to heat his oven, and the leaven to raise his dough, that the false principles which he introduced might infect the whole population. This prince, purposing to make his subjects relinquish their ancient religion, put, in a certain sense, the fire to his own oven, and mixed his dough with leaven. At first he used no violence, but was satisfied with exhorting them, and proclaiming a feast. This fire spread very rapidly, and the dough was very soon impregnated by the leaven. All Israel was seen running to this feast, and partaking in these innovations. But what shall become of the oven - the kingdom; and the bread - the people? The oven shall be consumed by these flames; the king, the princes, and the people shall be enveloped in the burning, <reference osisRef="Hos.7.7">Hos 7:7</reference>. Israel was put under the ashes, as a loaf well kneaded and leavened; but not being carefully turned, it was burnt on one side before those who prepared it could eat of it; and enemies and strangers came and carried off the loaf. See <reference osisRef="Hos.7.8">Hos 7:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.7.9">Hos 7:9</reference>. Their lasting captivity was the consequence of their wickedness and their apostasy from the religion of their fathers. On this explication <reference osisRef="Hos.7.4-Hos.7.9">Hos 7:4-9</reference>, may be easily understood.
entries.e367b256db7cf2dbdfa17e24801cb699188a3aeb: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen33717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33718" type="x-p"/> All their kings are fallen - There was a pitiful slaughter among the idolatrous kings of Israel; four of them had fallen in the time of this prophet. Zechariah was slain by Shallum; Shallum, by Menahem; Pekahiah, by Pekah; and Pekah, by Hoshea, 2 Kings 15. All were idolaters, and all came to an untimely death.
entries.e69056228beb055bf668865e3870e0c756af1d22: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen33718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33719" type="x-p"/> A cake not turned - In the East having heated the hearth, they sweep one corner, put the cake upon it, and cover it with embers; in a short time they turn it, cover it again, and continue this several times, till they find it sufficiently baked. All travelers into Asiatic countries have noted this.
entries.00a92d5e613e83fb176d1e72c49bacbbd7aa28aa: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen33719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33720" type="x-p"/> Gray hairs are here and there upon him, yet he knoweth not - The kingdom is grown old in iniquity; the time of their captivity is at hand, and they are apprehensive of no danger. They are in the state of a silly old man, who through age and infirmities is become nearly bald, and the few remaining hairs on his head are quite gray. But he does not consider his latter end; is making no provision for that eternity on the brink of which he is constantly standing; does not apply to the sovereign Physician to heal his spiritual diseases; but calls in the doctors to cure him of old age and death! This miserable state and preposterous conduct we witness every day. O how fast does the human being cling to his native earth! Reader, hear the voice of an old man: - <div eID="gen33720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33721" type="x-p"/> O my coevals! remnants of yourselves, <div eID="gen33721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33722" type="x-p"/> Shall our pale withered hands be still stretched out? <div eID="gen33722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33723" type="x-p"/> Trembling at once with eagerness and age; <div eID="gen33723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33724" type="x-p"/> With avarice and ambition grasping-fast <div eID="gen33724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33725" type="x-p"/> Grasping at air! For what hath earth beside? <div eID="gen33725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33726" type="x-p"/> We want but little; nor That Little long.
entries.157043c9daca6fcec60cfdfb84d9fc334db13741: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen33726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33727" type="x-p"/> The pride of Israel - The same words as at <reference osisRef="Hos.5.6">Hos 5:6</reference> (note), where see the note.
entries.8011fbf0ba764dcb7efb8344774700ca2997fc60: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen33727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33728" type="x-p"/> Ephraim also is like a silly dove without heart - A bird that has little understanding; that is easily snared and taken; that is careless about its own young, and seems to live without any kind of thought. It has been made, by those who, like itself, are without heart, the symbol of conjugal affection. Nothing worse could have been chosen, for the dove and its mate are continually quarrelling. <div eID="gen33728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33729" type="x-p"/> They call to Egypt, they go to Assyria - They strive to make these their allies and friends; but in this they showed that they were without heart, had not a sound understanding; for these were rival nations, and Israel could not attach itself to the one without incurring the jealousy and displeasure of the other. Thus, like the silly dove, they were constantly falling into snares; sometimes of the Egyptians, at others of the Assyrians. By the former they were betrayed; by the latter, ruined.
entries.43d76fd5ab49ab6f5266d83543d947476f520954: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen33729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33730" type="x-p"/> When they shall go - To those nations for help: - <div eID="gen33730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33731" type="x-p"/> I will spread my net upon them - I will cause them to be taken by those in whom they trusted. <div eID="gen33731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33732" type="x-p"/> I will bring them down - They shall no sooner set off to seek this foreign help, than my net shall bring them down to the earth. The allusion to the dove, and to the mode of taking the fowls of heaven, is still carried on. <div eID="gen33732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33733" type="x-p"/> As their congregation hath heard - As in their solemn assemblies they before have heard; in the reading of my law, and the denunciation of my wrath against idolaters. <div eID="gen33733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33734" type="x-p"/> Bishop Newcome translates: "I will chastise them when they hearken to their assembly." That is, when they take the counsel of their elders to go down to Egypt for help, and trust in the arm of the Assyrians for succor.
entries.8f99d5ddb745f3099f1de28a6c448744dbb8957a: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen33734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33735" type="x-p"/> Wo unto them! - They shall have wo, because they have fled from me. They shall have destruction, because they have transgressed against me. <div eID="gen33735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33736" type="x-p"/> Though I have redeemed them - Out of Egypt; and given them the fullest proof of my love and power. <div eID="gen33736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33737" type="x-p"/> Yet they have spoken lies against me - They have represented me as rigorous and cruel; and my service as painful and unprofitable.
entries.afea52876451163ca3ce09a9eff946f5eb331828: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen33737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33738" type="x-p"/> They have not cried unto me with their heart - They say they have sought me, but could not find me; that they have cried unto me, but I did not answer. I know they have cried, yea, howled; but could I hear them when all was forced and hypocritical, not one sigh coming from their heart? <div eID="gen33738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33739" type="x-p"/> They assemble themselves for corn and wine - In dearth and famine they call and howl: but they assemble themselves, not to seek Me, but to invoke their false gods for corn and wine.
entries.c94aedb77c4e3967be9e908c8002d957c16447d1: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen33739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33740" type="x-p"/> Though I have bound and strengthened their arms - Whether I dealt with them in judgment or mercy, it was all one; in all circumstances they rebelled against me.
entries.84d6623acba0c56befbc22c1ceb71b8f583d6b40: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen33740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33741" type="x-p"/> They return, but not to the Most High - They go to their idols. <div eID="gen33741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33742" type="x-p"/> They are like a deceitful bow - Which, when it is reflexed, in order to be strung, suddenly springs back into its quiescent curve; for the eastern bows stand in their quiescent state in a curve; and in order to be strung must be beaded back in the opposite direction. This bending of the bow requires both strength and skill; and if not properly done, it will fly back, and regain its former position; and in this recoil endanger the archer - may even break an arm. I have been in this danger myself in bending the Asiatic bow. For want of this knowledge not one commentator has hit the meaning of the passage. <div eID="gen33742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33743" type="x-p"/> Shall fall by the sword - Their tongue has been enraged against Me; the sword shall be enraged against them. They have mocked me, (<reference osisRef="Hos.7.5">Hos 7:5</reference>), and their fall is now a subject of derision in the land of Egypt. What they have sown, that do they now reap.  <chapter eID="Hos.7"/> <div eID="gen33743" type="x-p"/>

entries.3c984a7cfda63280e71c23054ffe183e5a8da0bf: Hos 7:1-3 <div eID="gen16225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16226" type="x-p"/> In the first strophe (Hos 7:1-7) the exposure of the moral depravity of Israel is continued. Hos 7:1. <hi type="italic">“When I heal Israel, the iniquity of Ephraim, reveals itself, and the wickedness of Samaria: for they practise deceit; and the thief cometh, the troop of robbers plundereth without.</hi> Hos 7:2. <hi type="italic">And they say not in their heart, I should remember all their wickedness. Now their deeds have surrounded them, they have occurred before my face.</hi> Hos 7:3. <hi type="italic">They delight the king with their wickedness, and princes with their lies.” </hi> As the dangerous nature of a wound is often first brought out by the attempt to heal it, so was the corruption of Israel only brought truly to light by the effort to stem it. The first hemistich of Hos 7:1 is not to be referred to the future, nor is the healing to be understood as signifying punishment, as Hitzig supposes; but the allusion is to the attempts made by God to put a stop to the corruption, partly by the preaching of repentance and the reproofs of the prophets, and partly by chastisements designed to promote reformation. The words contain no threatening of punishment, but a picture of the moral corruption that had become incurable. Here again Ephraim is not the particular tribe, but is synonymous with Israel, the people or kingdom of the ten tribes; and Samaria is especially mentioned in connection with it, as the capital and principal seat of the corruption of morals, just as Judah and Jerusalem are frequently classed together by the prophets. The lamentation concerning the incurability of the kingdom is followed by an explanatory notice of the sins and crimes that are openly committed. <hi type="italic">Sheqer</hi>, lying, i.e., deception both in word and deed towards God and man, theft and highway robbery and not fear of the vengeance of God. “<hi type="italic">Accedit ad haec facinora securitas eorum ineffabilis</hi>” (Marck). They do not consider that God will remember their evil deeds, and punish them; they are surrounded by them on all sides, and perform them without shame or fear before the face of God Himself. These sins delight both king and prince. To such a depth have even the rulers of the nation, who ought to practise justice and righteousness, fallen, that they not only fail to punish the sins, but take pleasure in their being committed.
entries.c84b9d5fbca3f49a2384e7eccc876c0f842ba8ec: Hos 7:4-7 <div eID="gen16226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16227" type="x-p"/> To this there is added the passion with which the people make themselves slave to idolatry, and their rulers give themselves up to debauchery (Hos 7:4-7). Hos 7:4. <hi type="italic">“They are all adulterers, like an oven heated by the baker, who leaves off stirring from the kneading of the dough until its leavening.</hi> Hos 7:5. <hi type="italic">In the day of our king the princes are made sick with the heat of wine: he has stretched out his hand with the scorners.</hi> Hos 7:6. <hi type="italic">For they have brought their heart into their ambush, as into the oven; the whole night their baker sleeps; in the morning it burns like flaming fire.</hi> Hos 7:7. <hi type="italic">They are all red-hot like the oven, and consume their judges: all their kings have fallen; none among them calls to me.” </hi>“All” (<hi type="italic">kullâm</hi>: Hos 7:4) does not refer to the king and princes, but to the whole nation. נאף is spiritual adultery, apostasy from the Lord; and literal adultery is only so far to be thought of, that the worship of Baal promoted licentiousness.
